claim: Azure Foundry Agent Service hosted agents expose a configurable idle timeout per agent version, from 120 to 3,600 seconds, defaulting to 900 seconds (15 minutes); when reached, the platform suspends the sandbox's compute and saves its state until the session is referenced again.
stance_target: production agent platforms implement quiet, automatic idle-triggered suspension as a first-class feature
scope_conditions: Azure Foundry Agent Service hosted agents
quoted_support: The agent version's idle timeout can be 2 through 60 minutes and defaults to 15 minutes. When the timeout is reached, the platform deprovisions compute and saves state until the session is referenced again.

claim: Stopping a hosted agent session terminates its running compute while preserving the persistent filesystem volume, distinct from deletion which permanently releases all resources -- and stopping an already-stopped session succeeds without error (idempotent).
stance_target: quiet self-termination should be a reversible 'stop/suspend' operation distinct from irreversible deletion
scope_conditions: Azure Foundry Agent Service session lifecycle API
quoted_support: Stopping a session terminates its running compute while preserving the persistent filesystem volume. Unlike deleting a session, the session is retained and you can resume it later. Stopping a session that's already stopped succeeds without error.

claim: Stopping a session uses the same generic shutdown sequence as any container teardown (redeploy, scale-in) with no dedicated 'session stopped' code path; if the agent's handler doesn't reach a safe checkpoint before the grace period elapses, a multi-turn conversation moves to a resumable 'suspended' state while a one-shot task record is deleted outright.
stance_target: graceful shutdown handling is a distinct engineering requirement from idle-timeout policy itself
scope_conditions: Azure Foundry Agent Service resilient task subsystem
quoted_support: If your handler doesn't reach a checkpoint in time, the framework forcibly ends the turn. From that point, the outcome matches an explicit cancel: for a multi-turn conversation, the chain moves to suspended and stays resumable; for a one-shot task, the record is deleted.

claim: Microsoft's own documentation explicitly warns that a manually-stopped session is NOT guaranteed to restart automatically even when its in-flight work was preserved for recovery -- the resume trigger is the responsibility of the hosting environment/application, not an automatic platform guarantee.
stance_target: audited absence: quiet self-termination architectures cannot assume automatic platform-level resume and must engineer their own wake/resume contract
scope_conditions: Azure Foundry Agent Service session stop/resume semantics
quoted_support: A session you stop yourself isn't guaranteed to restart on its own even when its work was left in progress for recovery. Check your hosting platform's documentation for how to explicitly resume a stopped session before assuming recovery happens automatically.

claim: Hosted agent sessions persist for up to 30 days, decoupling long-lived agent state from the much shorter idle-timeout window that governs compute suspension.
stance_target: session durability vs. compute suspension are independently tunable in production agent platforms
quoted_support: Sessions persist for up to 30 days.

claim: A dedicated administrative RBAC role ('Foundry User', carrying sessions/read and sessions/write data actions) is required to list, inspect, or act on sessions across all users on an agent for debugging, cost analysis, or incident response -- by default each caller sees only their own sessions.
stance_target: cross-agent/cross-user visibility into idle or stopped sessions requires explicit elevated access, relevant to fleet-wide auto-kill observability
scope_conditions: Azure Foundry Agent Service RBAC model
quoted_support: An administrator or automation that needs to work with every session on an agent - for debugging, cost analysis, or incident response - needs the Foundry User role on the Foundry project.
